newsitem.title: KYRGYZSTAN: Kyrgyzstan's debt rises but not critical - official.
newsitem.headline: Kyrgyzstan's debt rises but not critical - official.

text.p: Kyrgyzstan's official foreign debt serviced by the government reached $680 million by January 1, 1997, but it is not critical for the tiny former Soviet republic, a senior government official said on Monday.

Officials had put Kyrgyzstan's foreign debt at $609 million on October 1 last year. Kyrgyz debt to countries of the Commonwealth of Independent States -- mostly to Russia -- has risen to $194.7 million from $184 million in the period.
"Although Kyrgyzstan's foreign debt is growing, it is not as catastrophic as it might seem at first glance," deputy finance minister Alymbek Biyalinov told a news briefing.
"The proportion between the external debt and the state of the economy is in line with standard levels."
He said the external debt of the Central Asian state accounted for 39 percent of its gross domestic product (GDP), while the internationally accepted limit was 80 percent.
Servicing the foreign debt costs the republic of 4.5 million eight percent of GDP, while the critical level is 20 percent, Biyalinov said.
"Kyrgyzstan is a small open economy, and its growth must be accompanied by loans from abroad," Biyalinov said.
The Kyrgyz economy grew 5.6 percent in 1996, and officials target this year's economic growth at 7.2 percent.
Inflation has been curbed and is expected to drop this year to 17 percent from 31.4 percent in 1996.
